title: Similarity Preserving Adversarial Graph Contrastive Learning

problem.claim: Graph neural network models, particularly graph contrastive learning methods, are vulnerable to adversarial attacks involving perturbations to graph structure and node features.

gap.claim: Existing adversarially trained graph contrastive learning methods achieve robustness at the expense of preserving node feature similarity.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes the similarity-preserving adversarial graph contrastive learning framework, SP-AGCL.
SP-AGCL contrasts the clean graph with a node similarity-preserving view and an adversarial view.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that SP-AGCL achieves competitive performance on several downstream tasks.
The authors report effectiveness in scenarios involving adversarial attacks, noisy labels, and heterophilous neighbors.
The authors state that code is available in a GitHub repository.

narrative_sequence.summary: GNN models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that perturb graph structure and node features.
Graph contrastive learning methods are especially vulnerable because they depend on self-supervision signals from the attacked graph.
Existing methods use adversarial training within the graph contrastive learning framework.
These methods sacrifice node feature similarity preservation while achieving robustness.
SP-AGCL contrasts clean and auxiliary graph views, with reported competitive downstream performance and effectiveness across several scenarios.

source_observation.claim: Adversarial training can improve robustness while reducing preservation of node feature similarity.

interpretation.claim: Robustness objectives may conflict with representation-similarity objectives.

application.claim: When designing robust graph representation learning methods, evaluate both attack robustness and preservation of relevant similarities.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify when this trade-off occurs or whether it generalizes beyond the reported methods and scenarios.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify datasets, baselines, metrics, or numerical results.
The abstract does not describe the optimization procedure or model architecture in detail.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported results.
